newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialist willing to rule with Communists.
newsitem.headline: French Socialist willing to rule with Communists.

text.p: Opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin expressed willingness on Sunday to rule with Communists if his party wins a snap parliamentary election but said they must accept Socialist policies.

"Communism has disappeared, we found that in 1989" with the fall of the Berlin Wall, Jospin told Canal Plus television. "I think capitalism is showing itself to be arrogant. I think we need to have more balance, more democracy."
Opinion polls show the Socialists and smaller Communist party are trailing the ruling coalition for the May 25-June 1 National Assembly election.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe portrays the Socialists as hostages to an extremist Communist agenda -- the Socialists favour a single European currency from 1999, for instance, the Communists are bitterly opposed.
Asked if he would appoint Communist ministers if the two won enough seats to form a coalition, Jospin said:
"If they are able to accept the responsibility of a clear guideline set by French voters, and which will necessarily be that fixed by the biggest party on the left, why not?"
"I think that their problem is that they can't manage to decide in one way or another," he added.
Jospin, 59, is to meet Communist party boss Robert Hue on Tuesday to try to iron out differences.
Jospin, a white-haired former education minister, also blasted Juppe's leadership of the ruling coalition's campaign in the snap election.

"I thought he was the head of the campaign, sometimes I wonder if it's still the case," Jospin said. He said the premier "merited a better image but that he has this proudness, this hardness, this arrogance which I fear he may never shake off".

Opinion polls in late 1996 showed that Juppe was the least popular prime minister in modern French history amid record unemployment, weak growth and an abrupt shift to austerity to help qualify for the single currency.
Juppe's allies, aware of his unpopularity with voters, are steering clear of saying they want Juppe to stay on as premier in case of victory.
Juppe, 51, campaigned on Sunday in the south-western city of Bordeaux where he is mayor and is standing for election to parliament. He fired the starters' gun a the local marathon.
He was to appear in a television interview at 1700 GMT.

Jean-Francois Mancel, the number two in the Rally for the Republic Party (RPR) headed by Juppe, praised the premier's campaign and brushed aside questions of whether President Jacques Chirac would keep on Juppe if the centre-right wins.

"We've never had parliamentary elections praised the premier's campaign and brushed aside questions of to choose a prime minister...That question has absolutely no interest for the French people," he told Radio-J.
Former budget minister Nicolas Sarkozy, a member of the RPR, also stopped short of endorsing Juppe, saying "the decision about the choice of prime minister...belongs to Jacques Chirac."
If elected, Jospin said he would not seek to overturn Chirac's plans to scrap French military service but might extend a planned three-day course of civic instruction planned to replace it.
But he said the left would overturn tough laws cracking down on illegal immigration. He also said that he would seek to decriminalise hashish, admitting he had twice smoked it.
